claim: eLife has a policy to restrict requests for new experiments or analyses to those that can reasonably be completed in two months.
source: eLife has always taken a strong stand against reviewers and editors imposing additional work on authors, and it has been our policy to restrict requests for new experiments or analyses to those that can reasonably be completed in two months (see elifesciences.org/about/peer-review).
evidence: This is stated as an existing policy of eLife journal with a reference to their peer review guidelines.

claim: The two-month policy was meant to balance letting authors control their own science with the reality that sometimes additional experiments make papers stronger.
source: This policy was meant to strike a balance between the desire to let authors control their own science, and the reality that sometimes additional experiments make papers stronger.
evidence: This explains the rationale behind the existing policy.

claim: The two-month policy results in editors and reviewers comparing submitted manuscripts to an envisioned version with a few extra months' work.
source: But one result of this policy is that editors and reviewers naturally compare the submitted manuscript to an envisioned version of the paper that includes a few extra months' work.
evidence: This is an observation about the behavioral consequence of the policy.

claim: The comparison to an envisioned version with extra work almost always makes the submitted paper appear wanting.
source: This almost always makes the paper in hand appear wanting.
evidence: This is a stated consequence of the comparison behavior.

claim: Many authors will be unable to do additional experiments for the foreseeable future due to COVID-19.
source: However, given that many authors will be unable to do additional experiments for the foreseeable future, this dynamic must change.
evidence: This is an assertion about the impact of COVID-19 on research capacity.

claim: eLife is asking editors to accept without delay submitted manuscripts that can stand as eLife papers, even if they would be stronger with additional data.
source: We are therefore asking editors to accept without delay submitted manuscripts that in their judgment can stand as eLife papers, even if they feel that the manuscript would be stronger with additional data.
evidence: This is a new policy directive stated by eLife.

claim: For manuscripts that can stand as eLife papers but would be stronger with additional data, eLife will limit requests for revision to issues of clarity and presentation.
source: In such cases, we will limit requests for revision to issues of clarity and presentation.
evidence: This is a specific policy change being implemented.

claim: If work belongs in eLife but some conclusions require modest additional new data, eLife will ask for revisions that either alter the claims or make clear that conclusions require additional supporting data.
source: If the editors determine that the work as a whole belongs in eLife, but some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, we will ask for revisions that either alter the claims or make clear that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.
evidence: This describes a specific policy for handling papers that need modest additional data.

claim: Papers accepted with the expectation of additional experiments will have authors eventually carry out the experiments and report results either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or as a Research Advance in eLife.
source: If such revisions are made, the paper will be accepted for publication in eLife with the expectation that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.
evidence: This describes the process for follow-up work on accepted papers.

claim: Papers with potential but needing new data to meet eLife standards will be treated as normal revisions.
source: Papers which the editors judge to have potential, but where new data are needed to meet the standards of eLife, will be treated as normal revisions.
evidence: This describes how certain papers will be handled under the new policy.

claim: eLife will post manuscripts in revision to bioRxiv along with reviews and a formal declaration that the manuscript is 'in revision at eLife' at the authors' discretion.
source: We will, at the authors' discretion, post the manuscript to bioRxiv along with our reviews and a formal declaration that the manuscript is 'in revision at eLife' (which the authors can cite on their CVs and in applications for jobs and grants).
evidence: This describes a new option for manuscripts in revision.

claim: Authors can cite manuscripts 'in revision at eLife' on their CVs and in applications for jobs and grants.
source: We will, at the authors' discretion, post the manuscript to bioRxiv along with our reviews and a formal declaration that the manuscript is 'in revision at eLife' (which the authors can cite on their CVs and in applications for jobs and grants).
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the 'in revision' declaration.

claim: The policy changes will help authors whose research has been affected by the pandemic to publish their work without compromising eLife's standards.
source: We believe these changes will help authors whose research has been affected by the pandemic to publish their work without compromising eLife's standards.
evidence: This is eLife's stated belief about the impact of their policy changes.

claim: eLife typically allows two months for authors to submit revised manuscripts.
source: In recognition of the fact that revisions may take longer than the two months we typically allow, until the research enterprise restarts in full, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts.
evidence: This describes the existing time limit for revisions.

claim: eLife will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts until the research enterprise restarts in full.
source: In recognition of the fact that revisions may take longer than the two months we typically allow, until the research enterprise restarts in full, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts.
evidence: This is a new policy change being implemented.

claim: The suspension of the two-month limit applies to papers currently in revision and any submissions made during the pandemic.
source: This applies to papers currently in revision and any submissions made during the pandemic.
evidence: This specifies the scope of the policy change.

claim: Scientists studying COVID-19 and the pandemic have embraced preprint servers.
source: One of the most inspiring things about research in the age of COVID-19 has been the way that scientists studying the many manifestations of the virus and the pandemic have embraced preprint servers, and how this has greatly sped up the pace of research into understanding, preventing and treating the disease, and has also facilitated public understanding of what we are facing.
evidence: This is an observation about scientific behavior during COVID-19.

claim: The embrace of preprint servers has greatly sped up the pace of COVID-19 research into understanding, preventing and treating the disease.
source: One of the most inspiring things about research in the age of COVID-19 has been the way that scientists studying the many manifestations of the virus and the pandemic have embraced preprint servers, and how this has greatly sped up the pace of research into understanding, preventing and treating the disease, and has also facilitated public understanding of what we are facing.
evidence: This is a stated impact of preprint usage during COVID-19.

claim: The embrace of preprint servers has facilitated public understanding of COVID-19.
source: One of the most inspiring things about research in the age of COVID-19 has been the way that scientists studying the many manifestations of the virus and the pandemic have embraced preprint servers, and how this has greatly sped up the pace of research into understanding, preventing and treating the disease, and has also facilitated public understanding of what we are facing.
evidence: This is a stated benefit of preprint usage during COVID-19.

claim: eLife has always supported preprinting.
source: eLife has always supported preprinting, and we believe that author-driven, immediate publishing is the future of research.
evidence: This is a statement about eLife's historical position on preprints.

claim: eLife believes that author-driven, immediate publishing is the future of research.
source: eLife has always supported preprinting, and we believe that author-driven, immediate publishing is the future of research.
evidence: This is eLife's stated belief about the future of publishing.

claim: eLife will continue to let authors decide whether preprinting is appropriate for their manuscript.
source: We will continue to let authors decide whether preprinting is appropriate for their manuscript.
evidence: This describes eLife's policy on author choice regarding preprints.

claim: eLife will make posting to bioRxiv or medRxiv the default for all eLife submissions.
source: But to emphasize how important we think speed is when conveying new research, we will now make posting to bioRxiv or medRxiv – either by the authors or the journal – the default for all eLife submissions.
evidence: This is a new policy change being implemented.

claim: Authors will be able to opt out of preprint posting, but eLife will strongly encourage them not to.
source: Authors will be able to opt out, but we will strongly encourage them not to.
evidence: This describes the opt-out provision of the new preprint policy.

claim: It is essential that works get peer reviewed even after posting to a preprint server.
source: Of course, posting to a preprint server is only part of the process: it is still essential (arguably even more so) that works get peer reviewed, and this is the main function of eLife and other journals.
evidence: This is eLife's stated position on the importance of peer review.

claim: Peer review is the main function of eLife and other journals.
source: Of course, posting to a preprint server is only part of the process: it is still essential (arguably even more so) that works get peer reviewed, and this is the main function of eLife and other journals.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of journals.

claim: eLife has begun experimenting with a new system to attach eLife peer reviews to manuscripts on bioRxiv.
source: We have begun experimenting with a new system to attach eLife peer reviews to manuscripts on bioRxiv, and will roll this out more broadly as staffing and technology allow.
evidence: This describes an ongoing initiative at eLife.

claim: eLife will roll out the system to attach peer reviews to bioRxiv manuscripts more broadly as staffing and technology allow.
source: We have begun experimenting with a new system to attach eLife peer reviews to manuscripts on bioRxiv, and will roll this out more broadly as staffing and technology allow.
evidence: This is a stated plan for future implementation.

claim: It has always been eLife policy that the novelty of a finding is not diminished by related work published while a paper is under review at eLife.
source: It has always been eLife policy that the novelty of a finding is not diminished by related work published while a paper is under review at eLife (see 'Beyond scoops to best practices' and 'FAQ on preprints and scoop protection').
evidence: This describes an existing eLife policy with references to supporting documents.

claim: Many authors are posting preprints as a means to establish priority.
source: With many authors posting preprints as a means to establish priority, to avoid people feeling pressure to post their papers prematurely, we wish to emphasize that our scoop protection policy applies to preprints as well as peer-reviewed journal articles.
evidence: This is an observation about author behavior.

claim: eLife's scoop protection policy applies to preprints as well as peer-reviewed journal articles.
source: With many authors posting preprints as a means to establish priority, to avoid people feeling pressure to post their papers prematurely, we wish to emphasize that our scoop protection policy applies to preprints as well as peer-reviewed journal articles.
evidence: This is a clarification of existing policy.

claim: If eLife editors consider that work has been done simultaneously by multiple groups, they will not consider any group's efforts to have been rendered less significant by the posting of work from another.
source: Specifically, if our editors consider that work has been done simultaneously by multiple groups, we will not consider any of the groups' efforts to have been rendered less significant by the posting of work from another.
evidence: This is a specific policy statement about how simultaneous work is evaluated.

claim: The scoop protection policy is not a change in eLife's approach to submissions that report attempts to replicate previously published studies.
source: Note that this is not a change in our approach to submissions that report attempts to replicate previously published studies: we have always had a policy of publishing replications or failures to replicate that we regard as important, and we will continue to do so.
evidence: This clarifies what the policy change does not affect.

claim: eLife has always had a policy of publishing replications or failures to replicate that they regard as important.
source: Note that this is not a change in our approach to submissions that report attempts to replicate previously published studies: we have always had a policy of publishing replications or failures to replicate that we regard as important, and we will continue to do so.
evidence: This describes an existing eLife policy.

claim: eLife will continue to publish replications or failures to replicate that they regard as important.
source: Note that this is not a change in our approach to submissions that report attempts to replicate previously published studies: we have always had a policy of publishing replications or failures to replicate that we regard as important, and we will continue to do so.
evidence: This is a statement about continuing policy.

claim: eLife has been working with a global group of early-career researchers to increase their involvement in publishing for the past few years.
source: For the past few years eLife has been working with a global group of early-career researchers to increase their involvement in publishing.
evidence: This describes an ongoing eLife initiative.

claim: eLife carried out a successful trial of encouraging the use of early-career researchers as reviewers.
source: We carried out a successful trial of encouraging the use of early-career researchers as reviewers (see 'Reflections on focused inclusion in reviews at eLife'), and now do this across the journal.
evidence: This describes a completed trial with a reference to a document about it.

claim: eLife now encourages the use of early-career researchers as reviewers across the journal.
source: We carried out a successful trial of encouraging the use of early-career researchers as reviewers (see 'Reflections on focused inclusion in reviews at eLife'), and now do this across the journal.
evidence: This describes current eLife practice.

claim: eLife will bring forward its plan to invite early-career researchers to be eLife reviewing editors.
source: We will now bring forward our plan to invite early-career researchers to be eLife reviewing editors, as an effort both to increase opportunities for them to gain editorial experience, and to diversity and expand our editorial board.
evidence: This is a new policy change being implemented.

claim: Inviting early-career researchers to be reviewing editors is an effort to increase opportunities for them to gain editorial experience.
source: We will now bring forward our plan to invite early-career researchers to be eLife reviewing editors, as an effort both to increase opportunities for them to gain editorial experience, and to diversity and expand our editorial board.
evidence: This is a stated goal of the policy change.

claim: Inviting early-career researchers to be reviewing editors is an effort to diversify and expand eLife's editorial board.
source: We will now bring forward our plan to invite early-career researchers to be eLife reviewing editors, as an effort both to increase opportunities for them to gain editorial experience, and to diversity and expand our editorial board.
evidence: This is a stated goal of the policy change.

claim: eLife editors, reviewers and staff work incredibly hard to make eLife an amazing journal.
source: We ask for your patience on behalf of all the people who work incredibly hard to make eLife an amazing journal – our editors, reviewers and staff.
evidence: This is a statement about the work of eLife personnel.

claim: eLife editors, reviewers and staff have a lot going on during the pandemic.
source: Just like the rest of you, they have a lot going on and, while we hope to operate at peak efficiency, this may not be realistic for a while.
evidence: This is a statement about the circumstances affecting eLife personnel.
